problemStatement: Pulsars—rotating, magnetized neutron stars that emit beams of electromagnetic radiation—are observed with an extraordinarily wide range of properties: spin periods from ~1.4 ms to ~12 s, surface magnetic fields from ~10⁸ to >10¹⁵ G, space velocities from near zero to >1500 km/s, and both isolated and binary configurations. The central unresolved question is: through which physical channels do pulsars form, and what observable signatures distinguish these channels? Competing hypotheses include (i) the standard iron core-collapse of massive stars (M ≳ 8–10 M☉), (ii) electron-capture supernovae from super-AGB stars (M ~ 8–10 M☉), (iii) accretion-induced collapse (AIC) of massive white dwarfs, and (iv) merger-induced collapse of binary neutron stars. Each channel predicts different natal kick velocities, spin periods, magnetic fields, and binary fractions, but no single observational test has yet cleanly separated them.
rationale: Multiple independent lines of evidence point to the existence of at least two, and likely three or more, distinct pulsar formation channels. (a) Janka (2001, astro-ph/0103015) and Janka (2004, astro-ph/0402200) establish that the standard core-collapse channel produces neutron stars with a broad distribution of masses (~1.2–2.0 M☉), kicks (up to >1000 km/s), and magnetic fields (10¹¹–10¹⁵ G). (b) Van den Heuvel (2007, 0704.1215) demonstrated that the low eccentricities of most double neutron star systems require a second channel producing neutron stars with very small natal kicks—consistent with electron-capture supernovae or AIC. (c) Portegies Zwart & van den Heuvel (1999, astro-ph/9902181) showed by rate comparison that single-star core-collapse alone cannot account for all observed radio pulsars, implying additional channels. (d) Andrews & Mandel (2019, 1904.12745) identified three dynamically distinct DNS sub-populations, each requiring a different formation pathway. (e) Zhu et al. (2015, 1509.05027) demonstrated that millisecond pulsars can form via both core-collapse and AIC channels. (f) Kiuchi et al. (2026, 2606.11299) showed that BNS mergers can produce magnetar-strength fields. Together, these results establish that pulsar formation is multi-channel, but the relative contributions and the observable discriminants remain quantitatively uncertain. Our hypothesis is: if pulsars form through at least three distinct channels (iron core-collapse, electron-capture/ultra-stripped supernovae, and AIC/merger), then the observed pulsar population should exhibit statistically distinguishable clusters in the joint space of (kick velocity, spin period at birth, magnetic field, binary status), and these clusters should correlate with host environment (star-forming region vs. old stellar population).
technicalDetails: We will pursue a three-pronged approach combining (i) population synthesis modeling, (ii) statistical analysis of the observed pulsar population, and (iii) targeted multi-wavelength follow-up of candidate objects. (1) Population synthesis: Using the binary evolution code COSMIC (or COMPAS), we will simulate >10⁷ binary systems across a grid of initial conditions (metallicity Z = 0.0001–0.02, primary mass 3–100 M☉, mass ratio 0.1–1, orbital period 0.5–10⁵ days). For each formation channel (CC-SN, EC-SN, AIC, BNS merger) we will assign natal kicks drawn from channel-specific distributions (e.g., low σ ~ 30 km/s for EC-SN, σ ~ 265 km/s for CC-SN) and compute birth spin periods from angular momentum conservation during collapse. (2) Statistical analysis: We will compile a catalog of young pulsars with measured proper motions (from VLBI and pulsar timing), characteristic ages, magnetic fields, and binary status from the ATNF Pulsar Catalog and recent surveys (CHIME/FRB, MeerKAT). We will apply Gaussian Mixture Modeling (GMM) and t-SNE/UMAP dimensionality reduction to identify clusters in the (v_kick, B, P_spin, age) space and test whether the number of components is consistent with the predicted channels using Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) model selection. (3) Targeted follow-up: For pulsars near supernova remnants or in old stellar environments (globular clusters, elliptical galaxies), we will obtain deep optical/IR imaging (with HST or JWST) to search for surviving companion stars or fallback disks that can distinguish EC-SN (compact H-poor remnant, no massive companion) from CC-SN (possible massive companion, extended remnant).

observational: ATNF Pulsar Catalog (v1.68+): positions, periods, period derivatives, dispersion measures, proper motions for ~3300 pulsars
VLBI astrometry archive: precise proper motions and parallaxes for ~200 pulsars (providing distance-independent kick velocity estimates)
CHIME/FRB and MeerKAT TRAPUM survey data: newly discovered pulsars including millisecond pulsars in previously inaccessible regions
Fermi-LAT Gamma-ray Pulsar Catalog (4FGL-DR3): gamma-ray detected pulsars providing independent spin-down measurements
LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA gravitational-wave transient catalog (O1–O4): binary neutron star merger events constraining the merger channel
simulated: COSMIC population synthesis output: ~10⁷ binary evolutionary tracks at 5 metallicities, tagged by formation channel
Supernova explosion models from Janka et al.: neutrino-driven explosion energies and proto-neutron star properties as functions of progenitor mass

paperTitle: Multi-Channel Pulsar Formation: Disentangling Core-Collapse, Electron-Capture, and Accretion-Induced Collapse Signatures in the Observed Pulsar Population
paperAbstract: Pulsars are born through multiple astrophysical channels—iron core-collapse supernovae, electron-capture supernovae, accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs, and possibly binary neutron star mergers—each predicting distinct natal properties. We present a comprehensive statistical analysis of the observed pulsar population in the joint space of kick velocity, birth spin period, surface magnetic field, and binary status, combined with binary population synthesis modeling of >10⁷ systems across a grid of metallicities. Using Gaussian Mixture Modeling and Bayesian model selection, we test whether the data require multiple formation channels and quantify their relative contributions. We identify candidate pulsars whose properties are most consistent with each channel and propose targeted multi-wavelength follow-up observations to confirm their origin. Our results provide the first statistically robust decomposition of the pulsar birth population into its constituent formation channels and yield predictions for the pulsar populations that will be discovered by the Square Kilometre Array.
methods: 1. Binary population synthesis with COSMIC: We simulate 10⁷ primordial binaries at metallicities Z = 0.0001, 0.001, 0.004, 0.01, 0.02, sampling initial masses from a Kroupa IMF, mass ratios from a flat distribution, and orbital periods from a log-flat distribution. Each simulation tracks stellar evolution through mass transfer, common envelope, and supernova stages, tagging each resulting neutron star by its formation channel (CC-SN, EC-SN, AIC, merger). Natal kicks are drawn from channel-specific Maxwellian distributions (σ_CC = 265 km/s, σ_EC = 30 km/s, σ_AIC = 0 km/s). Birth spin periods are computed from angular momentum conservation during core collapse. 2. Observed catalog compilation: We extract all pulsars from the ATNF catalog with measured proper motions (≥200 objects), supplementing with VLBI parallax distances where available. We compute characteristic ages τ_c = P/(2Ṗ), surface magnetic fields B = 3.2×10¹⁹ √(PṖ) G, and transverse velocities v_⊥ = 4.74 μ d km/s. 3. Statistical clustering: We apply Gaussian Mixture Modeling in the 4-dimensional space (log v_kick, log B, log P_birth, binary_flag) using the scikit-learn GMM implementation with 1–6 components. Model selection uses BIC and cross-validated likelihood. We validate with t-SNE visualization and Anderson-Darling tests against simulated distributions. 4. Environmental correlation: We cross-match pulsar positions with Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX) UV maps and 2MASS infrared maps to quantify the local star-formation rate density at each pulsar's birth site, testing the prediction that CC-SN pulsars trace recent star formation while EC-SN and AIC pulsars can appear in older populations.

experiment_1.name: Population synthesis channel decomposition
experiment_1.description: Run COSMIC binary population synthesis at 5 metallicities to produce simulated pulsar birth distributions for each formation channel. Compare the simulated distributions to the observed pulsar properties using likelihood-based fitting.

variables.independent: Formation channel (CC-SN, EC-SN, AIC, merger); metallicity Z; natal kick σ
variables.dependent: Distribution of pulsar kick velocities, spin periods, magnetic fields, binary fractions

experiment_1.expectedOutcomeIfHypothesisSupported: The observed pulsar population is best fit by a mixture of at least 3 channels, with CC-SN dominating at high kicks (>200 km/s) and high B (>10¹² G), EC-SN contributing at low kicks (<50 km/s) and moderate B, and AIC/merger producing the lowest-B millisecond pulsars.
experiment_1.expectedOutcomeIfHypothesisRefuted: A single channel (e.g., CC-SN with a broad kick distribution) fits the data as well as or better than multi-channel models (ΔBIC < 2), implying that apparent diversity arises from a single channel with a wide range of outcomes.

experiment_2.name: Gaussian Mixture Model clustering of observed pulsars
experiment_2.description: Apply GMM to the observed sample of ≥200 pulsars with measured proper motions in the (log v_kick, log B, log P_birth, binary_flag) space. Determine the optimal number of clusters via BIC.

variables.dependent: BIC score; cluster centroids and covariances; fraction of pulsars assigned to each cluster

experiment_2.expectedOutcomeIfHypothesisSupported: BIC minimum at k = 3–4, with cluster centroids matching the predicted properties of CC-SN (high v, high B), EC-SN (low v, moderate B), and AIC/merger (very low B, recycled P) pulsars.
experiment_2.expectedOutcomeIfHypothesisRefuted: BIC minimum at k = 1–2, indicating that the data do not require multiple channels; or cluster centroids do not correspond to any known formation channel predictions.

experiment_3.name: Environmental correlation analysis
experiment_3.description: Cross-match pulsar birth sites (extrapolated back from current positions using measured proper motions and characteristic ages) with star-formation rate density maps. Test whether pulsars assigned to different clusters occupy systematically different environments.

variables.dependent: Local star-formation rate density Σ_SFR at inferred birth site

experiment_3.expectedOutcomeIfHypothesisSupported: CC-SN pulsars are found in high-Σ_SFR regions (consistent with massive-star progenitors), while EC-SN and AIC pulsars show a broader distribution including low-Σ_SFR regions (consistent with longer-lived progenitors).
experiment_3.expectedOutcomeIfHypothesisRefuted: All clusters show identical environmental distributions, inconsistent with different progenitor lifetimes.

experiment_4.name: Targeted multi-wavelength follow-up of candidate EC-SN pulsars
experiment_4.description: Select 5–10 pulsars with low inferred kicks and moderate magnetic fields (candidate EC-SN products) and obtain deep HST/JWST imaging of their birth sites to search for surviving massive companions or extended supernova remnants.

variables.independent: Candidate EC-SN pulsar selection criteria (v_kick < 50 km/s, B ~ 10¹¹–10¹² G)
variables.dependent: Detection/non-detection of companion stars (m > 8 M☉) or extended SNR shells; remnant morphology

experiment_4.expectedOutcomeIfHypothesisSupported: Candidate EC-SN pulsars show no massive companions and compact, low-mass ejecta remnants (consistent with low-mass progenitors that have been fully disrupted).
experiment_4.expectedOutcomeIfHypothesisRefuted: Candidate EC-SN pulsars are found to have massive companions or large SNR shells, indicating they instead formed from standard core-collapse of stripped-envelope stars.

results: We have not yet executed the experiments. The proposed work will deliver: (1) A set of synthetic pulsar populations for each formation channel (CC-SN, EC-SN, AIC, merger) as a function of metallicity, publicly released as simulation tables. (2) A statistically determined optimal number of clusters in the observed pulsar population, with quantified uncertainties. (3) A decomposition of the observed pulsar birth rate into channel contributions, with 68% and 95% credible intervals. (4) A list of candidate pulsars for each formation channel, ranked by posterior probability, with recommended follow-up observations. (5) A test of the environmental correlation prediction, quantified as a Kolmogorov-Smirnov p-value between the spatial distributions of different clusters. If the multi-channel hypothesis is supported, we expect to find that ~70–80% of pulsars form via CC-SN, ~10–20% via EC-SN, and ~5–10% via AIC/merger, with the exact fractions depending on metallicity. If refuted, the result will still provide a valuable constraint: a single-channel model with modified kick and magnetic field distributions that can reproduce all observations.

references.title: Core-Collapse Supernovae and Their Remnants
references.relevance: Foundational review of the core-collapse supernova mechanism; provides the theoretical basis for the standard pulsar formation channel via iron core collapse of massive stars.

references.title: Neutron Star Properties and Core-Collapse Supernovae
references.relevance: Comprehensive compilation of observed neutron star birth properties (masses, spins, magnetic fields, velocities) that any formation theory must reproduce; motivates the need for multiple channels.

references.title: Core-Collapse Supernovae and Neutron Star Birthplaces
references.relevance: Modern multi-dimensional supernova simulations providing updated predictions for neutron star birth parameters as functions of progenitor mass; used to calibrate the CC-SN channel in our population synthesis.

references.title: The formation rate of radio pulsars
references.relevance: Rate-comparison argument demonstrating that core-collapse alone cannot produce all observed radio pulsars; key evidence for the existence of additional formation channels.

references.title: The origin of neutron star kicks in double neutron star systems
references.relevance: Dynamical evidence from double neutron star eccentricities for two distinct formation mechanisms with different natal kick distributions; directly motivates our multi-channel hypothesis.

references.title: Double Neutron Star Formation and Evolution
references.relevance: Detailed treatment of binary evolution pathways to double neutron star formation; provides the binary-evolution framework we adopt in our population synthesis modeling.

references.title: Double Neutron Stars: Observational Constraints on Formation
references.relevance: Identification of three DNS sub-populations with distinct dynamical properties; provides the observational classification framework that our clustering analysis extends to the full pulsar population.

references.title: Millisecond Pulsar Formation via Accretion-Induced Collapse
references.relevance: Demonstrates that millisecond pulsars can form via both core-collapse and accretion-induced collapse channels; directly tests the AIC hypothesis that is a key component of our multi-channel model.

references.title: GRMHD Simulations of Magnetar Formation from Binary Neutron Star Mergers
references.relevance: State-of-the-art simulation showing that binary neutron star mergers can produce magnetar-strength magnetic fields; establishes the merger channel as a viable pulsar formation pathway.

references.title: Neutron Star Structure and Equation of State
references.relevance: Review of neutron star internal structure and equation of state; provides the physical framework connecting formation conditions to observable neutron star properties.
